title: Keep lamp oil and torch fuel away from children
summary: Lamp oil, kerosene and tiki-torch fuel are thin, oily liquids that a toddler can drink by mistake, and even a sip can slip into the lungs and cause a pneumonia that can kill. Store fuel locked away in its own child-resistant container, keep lamps out of reach, fill them away from children, and if a child swallows some, don't make them vomit: watch their breathing closely for the next day.

materials.item: Lamp oil, kerosene or torch fuel in its original child-resistant container
Lockable box, cupboard or shed for fuel
Marker and tape to label any lamp or can that isn't labelled
Funnel and a tray or rag for filling
Watch or phone with a seconds count, for counting a child's breaths

steps.text: Find every lamp fuel in the house: bottles of lamp oil (clear, coloured or scented), kerosene, tiki-torch fuel and fuel left in lamps and torches. Most lamp oil is paraffin; coloured lamp oil looks like a drink and clear lamp oil looks like water (Poison Control lamp oil).
steps.warn: Just a sip, or sucking a lamp's wick, can cause life-threatening lung damage; that is the warning EU and UK law require on lamp oil (UK REACH Annex XVII).

steps.text: Keep fuel in its original container until you pour it into the lamp (Poison Control lamp oil). Never in a drink bottle, cup or jar. If you must decant, use a proper fuel can, labelled with what's in it.
steps.warn: In a survey of 39 US parents, most children drank from the original container, and most of those containers had no child-resistant closure (Sheikh 2013).

steps.text: Close the child-resistant cap fully every time (CPSC Halloween lamps). In the US, most torch fuels and fuels for decorative or functional lanterns must be sold in child-resistant packaging (16 CFR 1700.14), which covers products with 10% or more petroleum distillates by weight and a viscosity under 100 Saybolt seconds at 100 °F. A broken or missing cap means a new container.

Store fuel up high, locked and out of sight of children (Poison Control lamp oil, Health Canada oil lamps). Out in a shed or fuel store is better than in the house; see [Fuel handling](#guides/safety_fuel_handling).

Fill lamps where children can't reach or watch, with the lamp cold and out, and put the fuel straight back in its locked place: Health Canada says any product holding liquid fuel should be kept out of sight and reach of young children or locked away (Health Canada oil lamps). Wipe up drips before the lamp goes back out. See [Wick lamps](#guides/skill_wick_lamps) for filling.
Keep lamps and torches, lit or not, out of children's reach, on a level, stable surface, away from curtains and anything that burns (Health Canada oil lamps, Poison Control lamp oil).
steps.warn: Health Canada advises against decorative liquid-fuel lamps in a home with children under five (Health Canada oil lamps).

steps.text: Check the lamp itself. In Canada a lamp's reservoir must carry warning labels, and if the fuel is required to be in a child-resistant container, so must the lamp be; some lamps sold in Canada have failed these rules (Health Canada oil lamps). Treat an unlabelled or uncapped lamp as one more open bottle of fuel.

Teach older children that lamps and their fuel are not toys, food or drink (Health Canada oil lamps). A tiki torch or patio lamp holds the same kind of fuel, so keep it and its fuel out of reach like the bottle. Tiki-torch fuel was the product children drank most often in one US survey (Sheikh 2013).

If a child has swallowed any, don't make them vomit (CHOP oils). Take off soaked clothes and wash oily skin with soap and water ([Fuel](#browse/hazards/fuel)). Keep the bottle so you know what it was (Poison Control lamp oil).
steps.warn: Vomiting gives the oil a second chance to get into the lungs (CHOP oils).

steps.text: Call a poison centre if phones work: 1-844-764-7669 (1-844-POISON-X) in Canada outside Quebec, 1-800-463-5060 in Quebec (Health Canada oil lamps), 1-800-222-1222 in the US (Poison Control lamp oil).

Watch the child closely for at least 6 hours, and keep checking for 24: coughing, choking, fast breathing, grunting or wheezing, chills, fever or unusual drowsiness can all mean oil is in the lungs (Poison Control hydrocarbons, Poison Control lamp oil, CHOP oils, WestJEM pneumonitis). See When no help is coming.
steps.warn: A child who coughs or chokes after swallowing lamp oil needs a doctor or nurse if there is any way to reach one (Poison Control lamp oil).

notes:
## Why it kills

Lamp oil, kerosene, torch fuel, lighter fluid and other thin oily liquids are hydrocarbons (Poison Control hydrocarbons). Swallowed, paraffin lamp oil is poorly absorbed by the gut. The danger is that it slips easily into the airway (Poison Control lamp oil). Oily, slippery liquids are more likely than most to be aspirated (CHOP oils), and the thinner and more volatile the liquid, the higher the risk (WestJEM pneumonitis). In the lungs it causes a chemical pneumonia: severe breathing trouble, and sometimes death (Poison Control lamp oil, Health Canada oil lamps, CPSC Halloween lamps).

It doesn't take much. The warning EU and UK law require on lamp oil says a single sip, or a child sucking on a lamp's wick, may cause life-threatening lung damage (UK REACH Annex XVII).

## Who it happens to

- US poison centres logged 23,536 calls about children and lamp oil products from 2000 to 2010. About 45% had symptoms, and 7 children died. The median age was 20 months and 91% happened at the child's own home; in the parent survey of 39 children, 77% said the child was not alone when it happened (Sheikh 2013).
- Cough or choking was the most common effect (34%) (Sheikh 2013).
- In a survey of 39 parents, tiki-torch fuel was the most common product (33%), then plain lamp oil (31%). Most children (59%) drank from the original container, and most of those (61%) had no child-resistant closure (Sheikh 2013).
- In 1991 CPSC warned about brightly coloured Halloween oil lamps after 10 reports of toddlers drinking the fuel; one child had died after drinking oil from a similar lamp (CPSC Halloween lamps).

Colour and scent make the problem worse in an obvious way: coloured lamp oil looks like a drink (Poison Control lamp oil). European REACH rules (still in UK law) ban colouring and perfume in lamp oils that carry the aspiration warning, and require them to be sold in black, opaque containers of 1 litre or less (UK REACH Annex XVII). In a small sample the US study found no link between colour or smell and how much a child drank, and it describes the European measures as having mixed results (Sheikh 2013), so locking the fuel away matters more than its colour.

Some scented oils for fragrance lamps also contain alcohols (Poison Control lamp oil).

## The rules on packaging

| Where | What the rules say |
|---|---|
| Canada | Oil lamps and their fuel fall under the Consumer Chemicals and Containers Regulations, 2001. The lamp's reservoir needs warning labels, and if the fuel must have a child-resistant closure, so must the lamp. Lamps brought in from abroad may not meet these rules (Health Canada oil lamps). |
| US | Liquid kindling and lighting fuels, including torch fuel and fuel for decorative or functional lanterns, with 10% or more petroleum distillates and low viscosity need child-resistant packaging (16 CFR 1700.14). |
| EU and UK | No colour or perfume in lamp oils labelled as an aspiration hazard; black opaque bottles of 1 litre or less; the "just a sip" warning on the label (UK REACH Annex XVII). |

A child-resistant cap only works when it's closed. Salvaged fuel often isn't in its first container, so whatever the rules said at the shop, the job of keeping it away from children is yours.

## The same danger from other fuels

Kerosene for heaters, lighter fluid, petrol, baby oil and mineral oil are on the same list (Poison Control hydrocarbons). Store heater kerosene the same way; see [Kerosene heater](#guides/skill_kerosene_heater) and [Fuel handling](#guides/safety_fuel_handling).

## When no help is coming

Most children who swallow lamp oil don't get seriously ill. In the US poison-centre data, 58.5% had a minor effect or none, about 1 in 100 (234 of 23,536) had a major effect, and 7 died (Sheikh 2013). Poison Control says a child with no symptoms after 24 hours should be fine (Poison Control hydrocarbons), but its lamp-oil page says to keep watching for symptoms over the next few days (Poison Control lamp oil). What you're watching for is the minority whose lungs are affected.

**Straight away**
- Don't make them vomit (CHOP oils).
- Take off oily clothes and wash the skin with soap and water ([Fuel](#browse/hazards/fuel)).
- If they have only swallowed it and have no symptoms, CHOP's poison centre says to offer a sip of water or juice (CHOP oils).
- Keep the container: plain paraffin oil, kerosene and scented oil with alcohol are not quite the same (Poison Control lamp oil).

**The next hours**
- Symptoms can start within a couple of hours or sooner (Poison Control hydrocarbons), but can be delayed by 6 to 24 hours (CHOP oils). Chest X-rays have been clear at first and shown lung damage 4 to 6 hours later (WestJEM pneumonitis, Poison Control lamp oil).
- Hospitals send home a patient with a small exposure after about 6 hours of watching, and keep one with symptoms for at least 24 hours (WestJEM pneumonitis). With no hospital, give the same watch at home: someone awake beside the child for the first 6 hours, then checks through the night.
- **Count the breaths** for a full minute while the child is calm. Fast breathing is 60 a minute or more under 2 months, 50 or more from 2 to 12 months, and 40 or more from 12 months to 5 years. Look for the lower chest sucking in with each breath (WHO IMCI). WHO's chart is a screen for pneumonia in children under five, not a lamp-oil protocol, so use it to judge how bad the breathing is. Write the counts down with the time, so you can see a trend.
- **Signs that oil is in the lungs:** coughing or choking, grunting or wheezing, fever, chills, fast breathing, trouble breathing, or unusual drowsiness (Poison Control hydrocarbons, CHOP oils, WestJEM pneumonitis, Poison Control lamp oil). The 3-year-old in Poison Control's case was drowsy, breathing fast and feverish (Poison Control lamp oil).
- **Danger signs:** a child who can't drink, vomits everything, is very drowsy or hard to wake, or has a fit (WHO IMCI). If you have a pulse oximeter, WHO's chart says to refer a child whose reading is under 90% (WHO IMCI).

**If the lungs are affected**
- Get the child to any doctor, nurse, clinic or hospital that is still working, however far. Severe cases may need a breathing tube and a ventilator (WestJEM pneumonitis).
- Until then, keep counting breaths and writing them down. In Poison Control's case the cough and fever had settled after about a day, and she went home a day after that (Poison Control lamp oil).
- Then find out how it happened and fix it: a lamp within reach, a bottle with its cap off, fuel in a drink bottle.
